This was to be demonstrated.

*Corollary.* From this, given the law of resistance and the difference *Aa* of the arcs *Ca* and *CB*, the proportion of the resistance to gravity can be gathered very nearly.

For if the resistance *DK* is uniform, the figure *BKTa* will be a rectangle under *Ba* and *DK*; and then the rectangle under 1/2 *Ba* and *Aa* will be equal to the rectangle under *Ba* and *DK*, and *DK* will be equal to 1/2 *Aa*. Therefore, since *DK* is the exponent <note>A mathematical representation of the magnitude of a force.</note> of the resistance, and the length of the pendulum is the exponent of gravity, the resistance will be to gravity as 1/2 *Aa* is to the length of the pendulum; exactly as was demonstrated in proposition 28.

If the resistance is as the velocity, the figure *BKTa* will be an ellipsis very nearly. For if a body, in a non-resisting medium, should describe the length *BA* in a complete oscillation, the velocity in any place *D* would be as the ordinate *DE* of a circle described with diameter *AB*. Accordingly, since *Ba* in a resisting medium, and *BA* in a non-resisting medium, are described in approximately equal times; and therefore the velocities at each individual point of *Ba* are very nearly to the velocities at the corresponding points of the length *BA* as *Ba* is to *BA*; the velocity at point *D* in a resisting medium will be as the ordinate of a circle or ellipsis described upon the diameter *Ba*; and therefore the figure *BKVT a* will be an ellipsis very nearly. Since the resistance is supposed proportional to the velocity, let *OV* be the exponent of the resistance at the middle point *O*; and the ellipsis *BRVSa*, described with center *O* and semi-axes *OB*, *OV*, will be very nearly equal to the figure *BKVT a* and the rectangle *Aa* multiplied by *BO* equal to it. Therefore *Aa* multiplied by *BO* is to *OV* multiplied by *BO* as the area of this ellipsis is to *OV* multiplied by *BO*: that is, *Aa* is to *OV* as the area of a semi-circle is to the square of the radius, or as 11 to 7 approximately. And for that reason, 7/11 *Aa* is to the length of the pendulum as the resistance of the oscillating body at *O* is to its gravity.

But if the resistance *DK* is in the duplicate ratio <note>The square of the ratio; resistance proportional to the square of the velocity.</note> of the velocity, the figure *BKVT a* will be almost a parabola having its vertex at *V* and axis *OV*, and therefore will be very nearly equal to the rectangle under 2/3 *Ba* and *OV*. Therefore the rectangle under 1/2 *Ba* and *Aa* is equal to the rectangle under 2/3 *Ba* and *OV*, and thus *OV* is equal to 3/4 *Aa*: and for that reason the resistance of the oscillating body at *O* is to its gravity as 3/4 *Aa* is to the length of the pendulum.

<summary>Newton establishes three corollaries for determining the ratio of resistance to gravity in a pendulum's motion, covering cases where resistance is constant, proportional to velocity, or proportional to the square of velocity.</summary>
<keywords>resistance, gravity, pendulum, velocity, duplicate ratio, ellipsis, parabola, Newton, mathematical physics</keywords>

You may also carry a dog's tongue placed under your big toe in your shoe, or if you carry a dried dog's heart with you, according to <term>Sextus</term> <gloss>Sextus Placitus, a 4th-century medical writer</gloss>. According to Pliny, you may carry a hare's fur or dung. Or you may carry the severed tail of a young weasel in your footgear, or give the dog a toad in a morsel of food; all these things serve to avoid the barking of dogs. Nigidius <note>Publius Nigidius Figulus, a Roman scholar and contemporary of Cicero</note> says that dogs will flee from the sight of a person all day long if that person removes a tick from a pig and carries it about for a little while. Oppianus <note>A 2nd-century Greco-Roman poet known for works on hunting and fishing</note> writes:

> If you carry but a small piece cut from the skin of a hyena,
> Both puppies and fierce dogs will instantly be struck,
> With a bitter terror, and they shall not bark at you thereafter,
> As you walk along, even if they had barked before.

### How a dog may be unable to run.

If you smear its wings <note>The author likely refers to the "armpits" or the leg-joints of the animal</note> with oil, it will be hindered in its running; it happens in this way.

### That a hawk may be courageous.

You shall encourage the bird against the prey so that it attacks large birds. Moisten the meat which it uses during hunting time with wine; or if it is a goshawk <note>original: "astur"</note>, give it a little vinegar. When it is about to fly, give it three morsels of meat soaked in wine, or pour wine into the beak of a young pigeon and then let it fly. In this way:

### You shall make partridges more pugnacious,

If you give them sprigs of <term>adiantum</term> <gloss>maidenhair fern</gloss> in their food, according to Pliny. And:

### Roosters become more pugnacious,

By giving them garlic in their food just before they are to fight. From this comes the very witty term in the Old Comedy, <term>eskordismenoi</term> <gloss>garlicked-up</gloss>, meaning someone who is vehement and excessively inclined toward a fight.

### Lest a bird fly high,

Pluck the tail feathers which direct its course upward, and thus it will fly in a circle below. If you wish:

### That a bird cannot fly at all,

Cut the upper and lower tendons of the wing; it remains without further harm, but the bird will not fly. In this way, they do not escape from aviaries.

<summary>This page provides folkloric and practical methods for hunters to silence barking dogs, manage animal aggression through diet—such as using wine for hawks and garlic for roosters—and physically prevent birds from escaping or flying high.</summary>
<keywords>animal husbandry, hunting lore, dogs, falconry, partridges, garlic, wine, Oppianus, Pliny the Elder</keywords>

By the confidence of his belief, such a man stands as far above other men as the sun surpasses the other stars with its light. For the sun itself illuminates the other stars not so much by the greatness of its power, as by its divinity and holiness. Believe that this sun, O Asclepius, is second to God, governing all other things and illuminating all worldly creatures, whether they are those that possess a soul or those that are inanimate.

For if the world is a living being <note>original: "animal mundus"</note> that is always alive, and was, and is, and shall be, then nothing in the world is mortal. Since every single part of a living thing exists within the world itself, as if in one and the same ever-living animal, there is no place for mortality. Therefore, God must be most full of life and eternity himself, if it is necessary for him to live forever. Consequently, just as the world is eternal, so too the sun is the perpetual governor of living things, or rather the source and dispenser of their entire vitality. God is therefore the everlasting governor of the living beings, or of the vital things that are in the world, and the eternal dispenser of life itself. Once and for all, he has dispensed life to all vital things by an eternal law, in this manner which I shall describe.

<summary>Hermes explains that the pious man excels among others like the sun among stars. He describes the world as an eternally living being governed by the sun under God's eternal law of life.</summary>
<keywords>piety, sun, Asclepius, living world, eternity, governor of life, divine law, immortality</keywords>

The seven spheres which are called "wandering" <note>the planets</note> have their own <term>ousiarchas</term> <gloss>leaders of essence</gloss>, that is, their own princes, whom they call Fortune or <term>Heimarmene</term> <gloss>Fate</gloss>. In this matter, all the philosophers have slumbered, laboring in vain to produce anything from it. Wherefore I make it known to all that the whitening <note>original: "dealbationem"</note> of which mention was made is drawn from a false foundation; by it, copper is falsely whitened but not transformed. The Sophists have mixed copper <note>original: "venerem"; literally Venus, the planetary correspondence for copper</note> masked and painted in this manner with twice its weight of silver <note>original: "lunæ"; literally Luna, the planetary correspondence for silver</note>, and sold it to goldsmiths and coin-makers. Ultimately, they transformed themselves into counterfeiters—not only those who sold it, but also those who bought it.

Some of the Sophists took red arsenic in place of white, and this itself resulted in a false art. For in whatever way it is prepared, it exhibits nothing but whiteness. Others proceeded further to common sulfur, which they cooked until yellow with vinegar, lye, or very sharp urine, day and night, until it emerged white. Afterward, they raised it from common salt and lime made of eggshells <note>original: "calce ouorum"</note> through sublimation; they cooked and sublimated it many times. Nevertheless, it always remained combustible, although white. With this, however, they attempted to fix crude mercury.

<summary>Paracelsus exposes the fraudulent use of arsenic and sulfur to create a superficial silver appearance on copper, leading to counterfeit currency. He argues that without understanding the "staining spirit," these chemical processes fail to achieve true metallic transmutation.</summary>

# Solutions to the arguments.
</margin>

The answer to the first argument is clear: there is no doubt that, just as men can kill with God's permission, so they can truly and realistically remove that member or others. But in such cases, the demons do not operate through the witches of whom mention is now being made. And by this, the solution to the second argument is also clear. But as for the point that because God further permits the <term>procreative power</term> <gloss>vim generatiuam</gloss> of witches for the sake of certain reasons, it should therefore also be permitted that the member be truly and realistically removed—this does not hold as a general rule. For if this were always the case, it would not happen by way of <term>witchcraft</term> <gloss>maleficii</gloss>, nor do witches even desire this when they perform such works, because they would not then have the power of restoring the member when they wish and know how. From this, it is clear that it is taken away not truly, but by a <term>glamour</term> <gloss>prestigiosa arte; a deceptive illusion</gloss>. To the third argument regarding the conversion of <term>Lot's wife</term> <gloss>vxoris loth</gloss>, we say: it was real and not by a deceptive art, whereas we are now speaking of the art of illusion. To the fourth, that demons can introduce certain substantial forms and therefore also take them away: it is said regarding the <term>magicians of Pharaoh</term> <gloss>magos pharaonis</gloss> that they made true serpents. Demons can produce some effects concerning certain imperfect creatures with the aid of some other agent, which they cannot do concerning humans, for whom God has greater care. According to that saying: "Does God have care for oxen?" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 9:9</note>. They can, however, always—as has been said—harm humans truly and realistically with God's permission, or else by a deceptive art. And by this, the solution to the final argument is also clear.

<margin>
# Question 10. Whether witches operate upon humans by transforming them into bestial forms through a deceptive art.
</margin>

Fourthly, the truth itself is declared regarding instances where humans are even transformed into beasts. Regarding how this might happen, it is argued that it is impossible for this to occur, according to the 26th Question, 5th Canon <note>A reference to the Canon Episcopi in the Decretum Gratiani</note>: "Whoever believes that any creature can be changed for the better or for the worse, or transformed into another species or another likeness, except by the Creator himself who made all things and through whom all things were made, is without doubt an infidel and worse than a pagan." And let us use the arguments of <term>Saint Thomas</term> <gloss>sancti Thome</gloss> in the Second Book of the Sentences, Distinction 8: Whether demons can impress upon the <term>bodily senses</term> <gloss>sensus corporales</gloss> by deluding them with <term>illusions</term> <gloss>prestigiis</gloss>. Where he first argues that they cannot. For that form of a beast which is seen must exist somewhere, but it cannot be only in the sense, because the sense does not have any <term>species</term> <gloss>mental image</gloss> except that which is received from things. And there is no true beast present, according to the authority of the Canon cited. Nor again can it be in the thing which is seen—as if a woman were seen as a beast—because two <term>substantial forms</term> <gloss>the essential nature of a thing</gloss> cannot exist in the same subject at one and the same time. Therefore, since that form of the beast which is seen can exist nowhere, no <term>deceptive illusion</term> <gloss>prestigiosa illusio</gloss> can occur in the eye of the beholder, since vision must necessarily be terminated by some form. Furthermore, if it were said that the form exists in the surrounding air, this cannot be; both because air is not receptive to any form or figure, and also because the same air does not always remain around that person due to its fluidity, especially when one moves. Also, such a transformation would thus be seen by everyone, which is not the case, since demons do not seem to deceive the visions of holy men, at the very least. Furthermore, the visual sense or visual power is a passive power. But every passive thing is moved by an active thing proportioned to it. The active thing proportioned to the sense is twofold: one as if originating the act, namely the object; the other as if conveying it, like the medium. But that form which is seen cannot be the object of the sense nor even the medium as if conveying it. Regarding the first, that it cannot be the object because it can be taken from no real thing, as touched upon in the preceding argument, since it is not in the sense as something received from a thing; nor in the thing itself; nor even in the air as if in a conveying medium, as touched upon in the third argument. Furthermore, if the demon moves the interior cognitive power, he does this either by presenting himself as an object...

<summary>This page addresses arguments regarding whether physical members can be truly removed or merely hidden by illusion, and begins a new inquiry into whether witches can transform humans into animals.</summary>

# QUESTION CXII

ON BOASTING. — Divided into two articles.

Next we must consider boasting <term>jactantia</term> and irony <term>ironia</term> <note>original: "jactantia — et ironia"</note>, which are parts of lying, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the *Ethics*, book 4, chapter 7.
First, regarding boasting, two things are asked: 1. to which virtue it is opposed; 2. whether it is a mortal sin.

## ARTICLE FIRST

Whether boasting is opposed to the virtue of truth.

To the first, the procedure is as follows. 1. It seems that boasting is not opposed to the virtue of truth. For lying is opposed to truth. But sometimes there can be boasting even without lying; as when someone displays their own excellence: for it is said in Esther 1:3: *Ahasuerus made a great feast... that he might show the riches of the glory of his kingdom* <note>The Vulgate reads: "the riches of the glory of his kingdom"</note> *and the magnitude and excellence of his power.* Therefore boasting is not opposed to the virtue of truth.
2. Furthermore, boasting is placed by Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great</note> in the *Morals*, book 23, chapter 4, near the beginning, as one of the four species of pride, namely when someone boasts that they have what they do not have; hence it is said in Jeremiah 48:29: *We have heard of the pride of Moab (he is exceeding proud), his loftiness, and his arrogance, and his pride, and the haughtiness of his heart. I know, says the Lord, his boasting, and that his strength is not according to it.* And in the *Morals*, book 31, chapter 7, near the middle, Gregory says that boasting arises from vainglory. But pride and vainglory are opposed to the virtue of humility. Therefore boasting is not opposed to truth, but to humility.

<margin>ARTICLE I. — Boasting properly so called is a vice by which someone externally carries themselves above what is actually in them. Although boasting, according to the use of the word, is also spoken of regarding the display of truth beyond the opinion or knowledge of others, as a vice of its kind (for thus only is it properly taken), it is not spoken of except as the opposite of truth, by way of excess; since only thus is it the name of a vice of its kind. For the display of truth beyond the knowledge of others is not evil of its kind, but is sometimes good according to necessity or utility, and sometimes evil because of an evil end (Cajetan).</margin>

(1) Vulgate: ...The riches of the glory of his kingdom.

<column-break/>

3. Furthermore, boasting seems to be caused by riches; hence it is said in Wisdom 5:8: *What has pride profited us, or what has the boasting of riches brought us?* But the superfluity of riches seems to pertain to the sin of avarice, which is opposed to justice or liberality. Therefore boasting is not opposed to truth.
— On the contrary, is what the Philosopher says in the *Ethics*, books 2 and 4, chapter 7, in both places, that boasting is opposed to truth.

I ANSWER that it must be said that boasting <term>jactantia</term> <gloss>a throwing or casting forth</gloss> properly seems to imply that a man extols himself in words. For those things which a man wishes to throw <term>jactare</term> far, he lifts up high. Now a person properly extols himself when he says something about himself that is above himself. This happens in two ways: — sometimes indeed someone speaks of himself, not indeed above what is in him, but above what men think of him; which the Apostle <note>St. Paul</note> avoids, saying in 2 Corinthians 12:6: *I forbear, lest any man should think of me above that which he sees in me, or that he hears from me.* — In another way, someone extols himself through words, speaking of himself above what is in him according to the truth of the matter. And because a man is more to be judged according to what is in him than according to what is in the opinion of others, it follows that it is more properly called boasting when someone carries himself above what is in himself than when he carries himself above what is in the opinion of others; although it can be called boasting in both ways. And therefore **boasting properly so called is opposed to truth by way of excess.**

To the first, therefore, it must be said that that argument proceeds from boasting insofar as it exceeds opinion.
To the second, it must be said that the sin of boasting can be considered in two ways: — in one way according to the species of the act, and thus it is opposed to truth, as was said in the body of the article and in Question 110, Article 2; — in another way according to its cause, from which it happens, if not always, yet quite frequently; and thus it proceeds indeed from pride as from an internal motivating and impelling cause; for from the fact that someone is inwardly lifted up above himself through arrogance, it follows for the most part that they boast of greater things about themselves externally, although sometimes someone proceeds to boasting not out of arrogance, but out of a certain vanity, and delights in this because they are such by habit. And therefore arrogance, through which someone is extolled above themselves, is a species of pride; yet it is not the same as boasting, but is most frequently its cause. And for this reason Gregory places boasting among the species of pride. Moreover, a boaster for the most part aims to obtain glory through his boasting; and therefore according to Gregory it arises from vainglory according to the nature of the end.

#### Whether more universal things are prior in our intellectual cognition

Regarding the third point, the procedure is as follows. It seems that more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition. For those things which are prior and better known according to nature are posterior and less known to us. But universals are prior according to the nature of our intellect. Therefore, universals are posterior in our knowledge.

Furthermore, composite things are prior to us compared to simple things. But universals are more simple than particulars. Therefore, they are known later by us.

Furthermore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the *Physics* that the thing defined first falls into our cognition, and the parts of the definition are less universal; for example, "animal" is a part of the definition of "man," and thus universals are known later by us.

Furthermore, we arrive at principles through effects. But universals are principles. Therefore, universals are known later by us.

But against this is what is said in the first book of the *Physics*, that we must proceed from universals to singulars.

I respond that it must be said that in the cognition of our intellect, two things must be considered. First, that intellectual cognition in some way takes its origin from sensitive cognition. And because the sense is of singulars and the intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the cognition of singulars be prior to the cognition of universals for us.

Second, we must consider that our intellect proceeds from potency to act. Whatever proceeds from potency to act first reaches an incomplete act, which is halfway between potency and act, before reaching perfect act. Perfect act, which the intellect reaches, is complete science through which things are known distinctly and determinately. Incomplete act is imperfect science through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For what is known in this way is known both in act and in a certain way in potency. As it says in the first book of the *Physics*: things that are more confused are first manifest and certain to us. Later, we know them by distinguishing their principles and elements distinctly.

It is manifest, however, that to know something in which many things are contained, without having proper knowledge of each of those things contained within it, is to know something under a certain confusion. In this way, one can know both a whole <note>a universal whole</note> in which parts are contained in potency, and an integral whole; for both wholes can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being distinctly known. To know distinctly that which is contained in the whole is to have knowledge of a less common thing; for example, knowing "animal" indistinctly is to know "animal" as it is, while knowing it distinctly is knowing it as either rational or irrational, which is to know "man" or "lion." Therefore, it occurs first to our intellect to know "animal" rather than to know "man." And the same reasoning holds if we compare anything more universal to something less universal.

<column-break/>

This order of cognition appears in the senses. For the sense judges more universal things before less universal ones, both in terms of space and time. For instance, when seeing something from a distance, we first perceive it to be a body, then we perceive it to be an animal, then a man, and finally Socrates. Similarly, it is clear that a child at the beginning distinguishes "man" from "not-man" before distinguishing individual men; children at first call all men "fathers" and later determine each one specifically, as is said in the first book of the *Physics*. This is because he who knows something indistinctly is still in potency to knowing it distinctly, just as one who knows a genus is in potency to knowing the specific differences. And thus, indistinct cognition is midway between potency and act.

Therefore, sensitive cognition of singulars is prior to intellectual cognition of universals. But within the intellect itself, cognition of the more universal is prior to cognition of the less common.

To the first objection, it must be said that "prior" can be considered in two ways. In one way, regarding the intention of truth. Since the intention of truth and the true itself have a relationship to many things, the abstraction of the intellect arrives at this last. As is said in the first book *On the Soul*, the universal is either nothing or it is posterior. But <term>Plato</term> <note>referring to the Platonic view</note> held universals to be substances, and in this consideration it would be true that particulars exist only by participation in the more universal subsistent things called Ideas.

In another way, it can be considered regarding the nature itself, such as "animality" or "humanity" as found in particulars. In this, there is a twofold order of nature. One is according to the way of generation and time, where those things that are incomplete and in potency are prior. In this way, the more universal is prior in nature, as is clearly seen in the generation of a man and an animal; for the animal is generated before the man, as is said in the book *On the Generation of Animals*. The other is the order of perfection or the intention of nature, just as act is simply prior to potency in nature, and the perfect prior to the imperfect. In this way, the less universal is prior in nature, just as "man" is prior to "animal." For nature's intention does not stop at the generation of an animal, but intends to generate a man.

To the second objection, it must be said that the more universal is compared to the less universal as a whole. The universal contains its parts in potency, such as "animal" containing not only "man" but also "horse." Therefore, "animal" considered in itself is prior in our cognition to "man."

To the third objection, it must be said that a thing can be known in two ways. In one way, absolutely as it is in itself. In another way, as it is a part of a whole. If we consider parts of a house like stones, we must first know the whole house in a confused way before knowing the parts. Thus it must be said that the defining parts, considered absolutely, are prior to the defined thing; otherwise, the defined thing would not be made known by them. But they are also parts of the definition.
